title: Large shocks can shape political preferences, risk attitudes, and institutional trust, especially when experienced young
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 32669 and 2025 Journal of Economic Literature review by Paola Giuliano and Antonio Spilimbergo
geography: Literature on recessions, inflation, trade, migration, wars, terrorism, pandemics, and natural disasters, including U.S. and cross-national evidence

denominator.unit: structured review of heterogeneous empirical literatures, not one pooled sample

preferences_and_beliefs.value: aggregate shocks affect political preferences, risk attitudes, and trust in institutions across the reviewed literature

life_stage.value: shocks experienced during young adulthood generally have stronger and longer-lasting effects

shock_type.value: negative economic shocks generally move preferences rightward, while non-economic shocks have more heterogeneous effects that depend on context

permanence_and_action.value: not one universally established permanent effect or direct preference-to-vote pathway

observations.method: Review of sociology, social psychology, and economics evidence across multiple shock types, with explicit discussion of empirical methods, limitations, cross-study comparability, mechanisms, life-stage timing, and persistence.
observations.uncertainty: This is a heterogeneous literature review, not a pooled causal estimate. Studies differ in shock exposure, population, outcome, timing, identification strategy, and follow-up. A reviewed association or pattern may not generalize across shocks, places, cohorts, or political systems.
observations.subgroup: People exposed to different aggregate shocks and at different life stages, especially young adulthood; reviewed subgroups and national contexts vary by study and are not one linked population.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed preference changes may reflect selective exposure, migration, media, institutions, cohort replacement, or measurement change. Economic shocks need not move every population rightward, and non-economic shocks can generate political responses that depend on threat, attribution, identity, and institutional context.

related_sources.claim: Published Journal of Economic Literature version, 2025, volume 63(2), pages 542-597.
IMF Working Paper version and review framing.

boundary: This record preserves a review-level pattern that shocks can shape preferences, risk attitudes, and institutional trust, with stronger effects in some young-adult exposure settings. It does not estimate one U.S. effect, prove permanence, identify one mechanism, or show that changed preferences became votes, protest, policy, or durable cultural identity.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: NBER abstract and published-version metadata reviewed for scope and headline conclusions; underlying reviewed studies are not collapsed into a new pooled estimate.
